interfaces.name: Sparse sequence model
interfaces.type_shape: Independent coordinates with a real-indexed density family. P_theta is the joint law; no common location or scale family is imposed at this level. Two original excerpts surround the separate sparsity convention.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Independent coordinates with a real-indexed density family. P_theta is the joint law; no common location or scale family is imposed at this level. Two original excerpts surround the separate sparsity convention.

members.statement_original:
For some $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)$ consider observing independent data $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ satisfying, for a family of density functions $(f_a:a\in\mathbb R)$,
\[
X_i\sim f_{\theta_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\tag{1}
\]
We write $P_\theta$ for the law of $X$ with parameter $\theta$ in (1) and $E_\theta$ for the corresponding expectation. Write $F_a(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_a(t)\,dt$ and $\overline F_a(x)=1-F_a(x)$ for the distribution function and the tail function, respectively.

evidence.location: Section 1.2 — sparse sequence model (1) — naming context

interfaces.name: Sparse asymptotic setting
interfaces.type_shape: At-most-s_n support class and global sequence regime. Specific parameter classes may require exactly s_n nonzero coordinates. Polynomial sparsity is a separate extra condition.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: At-most-s_n support class and global sequence regime. Specific parameter classes may require exactly s_n nonzero coordinates. Polynomial sparsity is a separate extra condition.

members.statement_original:
The vector $\theta$ is assumed to be sparse; that is, to belong to the set
\[
\ell_0[s_n]=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^n,\|\theta\|_0\le s_n\},\qquad
\|\theta\|_0:=\#\{1\le i\le n:\theta_i\ne0\},\tag{2}
\]
consisting of vectors that have at most $s_n$ nonzero coordinates, where $0\le s_n\le n$; throughout the paper we consider the sparse asymptotic setting where
\[
n\to\infty,\ s_n\to\infty\text{ and }n/s_n\to\infty.\tag{3}
\]

interfaces.name: Multiple testing procedure
interfaces.type_shape: Measurable binary decision vector, or sequence thereof. Null H_0,i means theta_i=0. The theorem infima are not restricted to threshold rules unless explicitly stated.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Measurable binary decision vector, or sequence thereof. Null H_0,i means theta_i=0. The theorem infima are not restricted to threshold rules unless explicitly stated.

members.statement_original: A multiple testing procedure is formally defined as a measurable function of the data $\varphi:x\in\mathbb R^n\mapsto(\varphi_i(x))_{1\le i\le n}\in\{0,1\}^n$, where, by convention, $\varphi_i(X)=1$ corresponds to rejecting the null $H_{0,i}$. As such, the procedure will depend on $n$, and with some slight abuse of terminology, when dealing with asymptotics in terms of $n$, a sequence of such procedures is sometimes simply referred to as a ‘procedure’ for short.

interfaces.name: False discovery rate
interfaces.type_shape: Expectation of the random false-discovery fraction, not a ratio of expectations. The denominator is truncated below by one.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Expectation of the random false-discovery fraction, not a ratio of expectations. The denominator is truncated below by one.

members.statement_original:
For any $\theta\in\mathbb R^n$ and any procedure $\varphi$, the false discovery rate (FDR) and the false discovery proportion (FDP) of $\varphi$ at the parameter $\theta$ are respectively defined as
\[
\operatorname{FDR}(\theta,\varphi)=E_\theta[\operatorname{FDP}(\theta,\varphi)],\qquad
\operatorname{FDP}(\theta,\varphi)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{\theta_i=0\}\varphi_i(X)}{1\vee\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi_i(X)}.\tag{5}
\]

interfaces.name: False negative rate
interfaces.type_shape: Expected missed-signal fraction, divided by the true support size truncated below by one. This differs from a false-omission proportion among accepted hypotheses.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Expected missed-signal fraction, divided by the true support size truncated below by one. This differs from a false-omission proportion among accepted hypotheses.

members.statement_original:
The false negative rate (FNR) at $\theta$ is here defined as (see, e.g., [5])
\[
\operatorname{FNR}(\theta,\varphi)=E_\theta\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{\theta_i\ne0\}(1-\varphi_i(X))}{1\vee\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{\theta_i\ne0\}}\right].\tag{6}
\]

interfaces.name: Combined risk
interfaces.type_shape: Sum of the two risks with their different denominators. Do not replace it by Hamming risk or by FNR alone.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Sum of the two risks with their different denominators. Do not replace it by Hamming risk or by FNR alone.

members.statement_original:
The (multiple testing) combined risk at $\theta\in\mathbb R^n$ of a procedure $\varphi$ is the sum
\[
\mathfrak R(\theta,\varphi)=\operatorname{FDR}(\theta,\varphi)+\operatorname{FNR}(\theta,\varphi).
\]

interfaces.name: Minimax multiple testing risk
interfaces.type_shape: Infimum over all measurable procedures, followed by worst-case parameter risk. FNR-only and classification minimax expressions are separately bound in their theorem statements.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Infimum over all measurable procedures, followed by worst-case parameter risk. FNR-only and classification minimax expressions are separately bound in their theorem statements.

members.statement_original:
To investigate questions of optimality, a natural benchmark is the minimax multiple testing risk, defined as
\[
\mathfrak R(\Theta)=\inf_\varphi\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathfrak R(\theta,\varphi),\tag{7}
\]
where the infimum is over all multiple testing procedures and the parameter set $\Theta$ is some appropriate subset of $\ell_0[s_n]$.

interfaces.name: Gaussian location model
interfaces.type_shape: Independent standard-variance Gaussian location noise. It is a particular model, not an additional condition on all general-noise results.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Independent standard-variance Gaussian location noise. It is a particular model, not an additional condition on all general-noise results.

members.statement_original:
The prototypical example to have in mind is the Gaussian location model, under which $f_a$ is the density of the distribution $\mathcal N(a,1)$, so that
\[
X_i=\theta_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\tag{4}
\]

interfaces.name: Beta-min type condition
interfaces.type_shape: Two original excerpts defining the beta-min class and its boundary parametrization. The initial domain a in R and later prose a>0 are both retained. Theorem 7 uses a separately archived union over support sizes without changing a_b.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Two original excerpts defining the beta-min class and its boundary parametrization. The initial domain a in R and later prose a>0 are both retained. Theorem 7 uses a separately archived union over support sizes without changing a_b.

members.statement_original:
To evaluate the minimax risk, we define a class of configurations for $\theta$ that measures how the alternatives are separated from the null hypothesis: for a given $a\in\mathbb R$, set
\[
\Theta=\Theta(a,s_n)=\{\theta\in\ell_0[s_n]:|\theta_i|\ge a\text{ for }i\in S_\theta,\ |S_\theta|=s_n\},\tag{9}
\]
where $S_\theta=\{i:\theta_i\ne0\}$ denotes the support of $\theta$ (recall $\ell_0[s_n]$ is defined by (2)). This choice corresponds to a so-called beta-min type condition, meaning that all intensities of nonzero coefficients are required to be above a certain value $a>0$.

We identify here a sharp formulation for this boundary, by considering for $b\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\Theta_b=\Theta(a_b,s_n),\qquad a_b=\sqrt{2\log(n/s_n)}+b,\tag{10}
\]
with $\Theta(a,s_n)$ as in (9).

interfaces.name: Polynomial sparsity assumption
interfaces.type_shape: Extra polynomial upper bound with an unknown exponent below one, distinct from s_n/n tending to zero. Branch applicability is recorded per theorem.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Extra polynomial upper bound with an unknown exponent below one, distinct from s_n/n tending to zero. Branch applicability is recorded per theorem.

members.statement_original:
Some will require an additional polynomial sparsity assumption: for some unknown $c<1$,
\[
s_n\lesssim n^c.\tag{12}
\]

interfaces.name: Benjamini–Hochberg procedure
interfaces.type_shape: Main-text description only. Exact threshold/intersection conventions and formula S-18 are deferred to the excluded supplement and remain unresolved; do not substitute a textbook convention.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Main-text description only. Exact threshold/intersection conventions and formula S-18 are deferred to the excluded supplement and remain unresolved; do not substitute a textbook convention.

members.statement_original: First, probably the most widely used multiple testing procedure is the so-called Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, introduced in [9]. For some level $\alpha$, it is given by $\varphi_\alpha^{BH}=(\mathbf1\{|X_i|\ge\widehat t\})_{1\le i\le n}$ where the threshold $\widehat t=\widehat t(\alpha)$ is defined as a specific intersection point between the empirical upper-tail distribution function of the $X_i$'s and a quantile curve of the noise distributions (see Section S-7 for details).

interfaces.name: Empirical Bayes calibration
interfaces.type_shape: Retain the strict posterior-probability threshold. The particular slab, prior weights and marginal-likelihood optimization domain are not given in this main-text passage; S-29 remains a supplement-only reference.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Retain the strict posterior-probability threshold. The particular slab, prior weights and marginal-likelihood optimization domain are not given in this main-text passage; S-29 remains a supplement-only reference.

members.statement_original: The second procedure uses Bayesian $\ell$-values (often also called local FDR values) with an empirical Bayes calibration. For a particular spike-and-slab prior $\Pi_w$ on $\mathbb R^n$ (see Section S-8 for details), we consider the empirical Bayes $\ell$-value procedure defined by thresholding posterior probabilities of null hypotheses at some specified level $t\in(0,1)$, i.e., $\varphi_t^{\widehat\ell}=(\mathbf1\{\Pi_{\widehat w}(\theta_i=0\mid X)<t\})_{1\le i\le n}$, where $\widehat w$ is the marginal maximum likelihood estimator for $w$, as in [36, 35].

interfaces.name: Sparsity-preserving
interfaces.type_shape: Uniform high-probability control of rejection count up to the factor A_n. It is neither a deterministic rejection cap nor an expected-count bound.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uniform high-probability control of rejection count up to the factor A_n. It is neither a deterministic rejection cap nor an expected-count bound.

members.statement_original:
We say that a multiple-testing procedure $\varphi=\varphi(X)\in\{0,1\}^n$ (or strictly, a sequence of such procedures, indexed by $n$), is sparsity-preserving over $\Theta=(\Theta_n)_n$ (with $\Theta_n\subset\ell_0[s_n]$) up to a multiplicative factor $A=(A_n)_n$ if, as $n\to\infty$,
\[
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_n}P_\theta\left[\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi_i(X)>A_ns_n\right]=o(1).\tag{14}
\]
We denote by $\mathcal S_A(\Theta)=\mathcal S_A((s_n)_n,\Theta)$ the set of all such procedure sequences.

interfaces.name: Assumption 1
interfaces.type_shape: Common part of Assumption 1; one of separately preserved branches A or B is required, not both. The Lipschitz constant is common to every F_a, and the threshold sequences are positive.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Common part of Assumption 1; one of separately preserved branches A or B is required, not both. The Lipschitz constant is common to every F_a, and the threshold sequences are positive.

members.statement_original:
There exists a constant $L$ such that each $F_a$ is $L$-Lipschitz. There exist sequences of positive numbers $a_n^*\to\infty$, $\delta_n\to0$ such that
\[
(n/s_n)\overline F_0(a_n^*-\delta_n)\to\infty,\tag{16}
\]
\[
(n/s_n)\overline F_0(a_n^*)\to0.\tag{17}
\]
The density $f_0$ is continuous and positive on $\mathbb R$. Further assume one of

interfaces.name: Assumption 1A
interfaces.type_shape: Location-type reflection and stochastic/likelihood-ratio monotonicity branch. The likelihood-ratio requirement is for a>0 and all real x; no strictness is added to increasing.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Location-type reflection and stochastic/likelihood-ratio monotonicity branch. The likelihood-ratio requirement is for a>0 and all real x; no strictness is added to increasing.

members.statement_original:
A. $f_{-a}(-x)=f_a(x)$ for $a,x\in\mathbb R$, $\overline F_a(x)$ is increasing in $a\in\mathbb R$ and, for $a>0$,
\[
f_a(x)/f_0(x)\text{ is increasing in }x\in\mathbb R.\tag{18}
\]

interfaces.name: Assumption 1B
interfaces.type_shape: Even-in-observation densities and positive-half-line monotonicity. The source does not explicitly impose f_{-a}=f_a in this branch; do not silently insert parameter-sign invariance.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Even-in-observation densities and positive-half-line monotonicity. The source does not explicitly impose f_{-a}=f_a in this branch; do not silently insert parameter-sign invariance.

members.statement_original:
B. $f_a(-x)=f_a(x)$ for all $a,x\in\mathbb R$, $\overline F_a(x)$ is increasing in $a>0$ for $x>0$, and for $a\ne0$
\[
f_a(x)/f_0(x)\text{ is increasing in }x>0.\tag{19}
\]

interfaces.name: Subbotin
interfaces.type_shape: Original model definition and threshold convention. Its assertion that Assumption 1A holds is a source claim, not an extra assumption needed to state Theorem 8. L_zeta is the density normalizer; Laplace noise is excluded.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original model definition and threshold convention. Its assertion that Assumption 1A holds is a source claim, not an extra assumption needed to state Theorem 8. L_zeta is the density normalizer; Laplace noise is excluded.

members.statement_original:
Assumption 1A holds with $a_n^*=(\zeta\log(n/s_n))^{1/\zeta}$ for the Subbotin (generalised Gaussian) location model, with $f_a$ denoting the law of $X=a+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\phi_\zeta$,
\[
\phi_\zeta(x)=L_\zeta^{-1}e^{-|x|^\zeta/\zeta},\qquad\zeta>1;\tag{20}
\]
see Lemma S-1. In particular, this model includes standard Gaussian noise as the case $\zeta=2$, while the excluded case $\zeta=1$ would correspond to Laplace noise. In this setting we will write $\overline\Phi_\zeta(x)=\int_x^\infty\phi_\zeta(t)\,dt$ and $\Phi_\zeta=1-\overline\Phi_\zeta$. Note that when we write $a_n^*$ in reference to the Subbotin model, we will mean the value $(\zeta\log(n/s_n))^{1/\zeta}$ except where specified otherwise.

interfaces.name: More general parameter set
interfaces.type_shape: Existential matching of positive lower strengths to distinct signal coordinates. Positions and signs remain unknown; strengths need not be equal or in source order.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Existential matching of positive lower strengths to distinct signal coordinates. Positions and signs remain unknown; strengths need not be equal or in source order.

members.statement_original:
In this section, we also consider a more general parameter set, with different signal strengths. For a vector $\boldsymbol a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{s_n})$ (implicitly indexed by $n$) with $a_j>0$ for $1\le j\le s_n$, define
\[
\Theta(\boldsymbol a,s_n)=\{\theta\in\ell_0[s_n]:\exists i_1,\ldots,i_{s_n}\text{ all distinct},\ |\theta_{i_j}|\ge a_j,\ 1\le j\le s_n\}.\tag{21}
\]

interfaces.name: Measure of the (lack of) signal strength
interfaces.type_shape: The average uses CDFs at the critical threshold. Branch A risk is Lambda; branch B risk is 2 Lambda-1. Preserve the parameter-sign convention and do not silently make the two branches equivalent.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: The average uses CDFs at the critical threshold. Branch A risk is Lambda; branch B risk is 2 Lambda-1. Preserve the parameter-sign convention and do not silently make the two branches equivalent.

members.statement_original:
A key quantity is
\[
\Lambda_n(\boldsymbol a)=s_n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{s_n}F_{a_j}(a_n^*);\tag{22}
\]
this can be seen roughly as a measure of the (lack of) signal strength for the parameter set $\Theta(\boldsymbol a,s_n)$. In a slight abuse of notation, if $\theta$ is a vector whose non-zero entries have absolute values $a_1,\ldots,a_{s_n}$ and recalling the notation $S_\theta=\{i:\theta_i\ne0\}$, we also write
\[
\Lambda_n(\theta)=s_n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_\theta}F_{|\theta_i|}(a_n^*).\tag{23}
\]

source_keywords.label: Measure of the (lack of) signal strength

interfaces.name: Condition on the level
interfaces.type_shape: Theta-dependent interval for the level. Theorem 5 uniform/o(1) assertions require careful source-scope notes; the printed interval alone permits nonvanishing levels. Preserve the branch-B replacement convention separately.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Theta-dependent interval for the level. Theorem 5 uniform/o(1) assertions require careful source-scope notes; the printed interval alone permits nonvanishing levels. Preserve the branch-B replacement convention separately.

members.statement_original:
Let us introduce the following condition on the level $\alpha=\alpha_n$ of the BH procedure:
\[
\frac{3n\overline F_0(a_n^*)}{s_n(1-\Lambda_n(\theta))}\le\alpha_n\le\min\left\{1,\frac{n\overline F_0(a_n^*-\delta_n)}{s_n}\right\}\qquad\text{for }n\text{ large enough}.\tag{24}
\]

interfaces.name: Classification (Hamming) loss
interfaces.type_shape: Unnormalized Hamming count. Theorem 7 divides its expectation by s_n; Theorems 8 and 9 divide by n^(1-beta). It is not the combined testing risk.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Unnormalized Hamming count. Theorem 7 divides its expectation by s_n; Theorems 8 and 9 divide by n^(1-beta). It is not the combined testing risk.

members.statement_original:
The classification (Hamming) loss in terms of classes $\{0\}$ and $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is defined by
\[
\mathrm L_{\mathrm C}(\theta,\varphi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\mathbf1\{\theta_i=0\}\mathbf1\{\varphi_i\ne0\}+\mathbf1\{\theta_i\ne0\}\mathbf1\{\varphi_i=0\}\right).\tag{30}
\]

interfaces.name: Parameter space of large signals
interfaces.type_shape: Unknown support size within a fixed proportional range and coordinatewise lower amplitude. The constants a,b here are unrelated to the earlier boundary offset b or strength vector. Signals may have unequal magnitudes.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Unknown support size within a fixed proportional range and coordinatewise lower amplitude. The constants a,b here are unrelated to the earlier boundary offset b or strength vector. Signals may have unequal magnitudes.

members.statement_original:
Let us first formally introduce an appropriate parameter space of large signals. For some $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\zeta>1$, and $r>\beta$, for fixed $0<a<b$, define
\[
\Theta(r,\beta)=\bigcup_{s_n\in[an^{1-\beta},bn^{1-\beta}]}\{\theta\in\ell_0[s_n]:|S_\theta|=s_n,\ |\theta_i|\ge M(r)\text{ for all }i\in S_\theta\},\tag{32}
\]
\[
M=M(r)=(\zeta r\log n)^{1/\zeta}.\tag{33}
\]

D6.D5: The second summand is the false negative rate.

D7.D2: The parameter set is a subset of the sparse class.

D12.D1: The posterior and marginal likelihood depend on the observation model.

D13.D2: The parameter sets are contained in the sparse classes with sizes s_n.
D13.D1: The overshoot probability is evaluated under P_theta.
